text: Every Python journey starts with printing a simple message — the print function is how your program talks to the world.
Whatever you put inside the parentheses and quotes gets displayed on the screen, exactly as you wrote it.
Next we store a piece of text, the string Python, inside a variable we're calling name.
A variable is just a labeled box — you put a value in once, then reuse it by name as many times as you like.
[chuckle] Now the fun part, an f-string. Put an f before the opening quote, and Python lets you drop variables right inside the text.
Anything inside the curly braces gets replaced with the variable's actual value the moment the line runs.
[sigh] Lines that start with a hash are comments — Python skips them entirely, they're just notes for anyone reading your code.
Variables aren't limited to text — here we store a number, a float, and interpolate it into another f-string just as easily.
And that's your first toolkit — print to show output, variables to store data, and f-strings to combine them. [laugh] Three tools you'll use in almost every program you ever write.
Next video: variables and assignment. Comment the topic you want after that.
